title: Chapter 1 – Computer Structure
description: What's inside the box, what runs on it, and how you talk to it — the foundation every other chapter sits on.
subject: IGCSE ICT

cards.back: A device that receives input, processes it, then produces output.

cards.front: The basic cycle: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Input – Data goes in
2. Process – The CPU works on it
3. Output – Results come out

cards.front: A computer has two components: what are the parts?
cards.back:
Hardware:
• Anything you can physically touch
Software:
• Any program or set of instructions
The physical components that make up a computer system.

External — visible to the user:
• Mouse
• Keyboard
• Monitor
• Printer
• Scanner
• Speakers
• Webcam
Internal — inside the computer:
• CPU / Processor
• Motherboard — lets hardware communicate
• RAM and ROM
• Graphics card (GPU) — visual output
• Sound card — audio in and out
• Internal HDD / SSD — stores OS and files
Hardware that processes instructions to produce an output.

Controls: all computer operations
Controls: input and output devices
Controls: movement of data
Executes: instructions from hardware and software
Carries out: calculations
Makes: logical decisions

Control Unit (CU):
• Controls interactions between CPU parts
• Fetches, decodes and manages execution of instructions
Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU):
• Performs calculations: + − × ÷
• Makes logical decisions: =, >, <
Internal memory directly accessible by the CPU. Also called primary or internal memory.

cards.front: Main memory: what are the parts?
cards.back:
RAM — Random Access Memory:
• Volatile · temporary
• Can be read and written
• Stores instructions, software, data and OS parts currently in use
ROM — Read Only Memory:
• Non-volatile · permanent
• Can only be read
• Stores start-up instructions (e.g. BIOS)

cards.front: Does it survive a power cut?
cards.back:
RAM: Contents lost
ROM: Contents kept
Backing storage: Contents kept

RAM: Volatile
ROM: Non-volatile

RAM: Temporary
ROM: Permanent

RAM: Read and write
ROM: Read only

RAM: Data, software, instructions and OS parts in use
ROM: Start-up instructions when switched on

RAM: Tends to be greater
ROM: Tends to be smaller
A program that carries out a hardware check to find out whether all devices are present and functional.

Non-volatile: Stores data permanently
Not CPU-direct: So slower than main memory
Used for: Files, software, moving data to another computer

cards.front: Your laptop loses an unsaved document in a power cut. Which memory held it?
cards.back: RAM — it's volatile, so everything in it vanishes without power.
Programs for controlling the operation of a computer and for processing electronic data.

Application — for the user:
• Word processor
• Spreadsheet
• Database management system
• Graphics / video / audio editing
• Apps and applets
System — for the computer:
• Operating system
• Device driver
• Compiler
• Linker
• Utilities (antivirus, disk repair…)

cards.front: System software, explained: Software vs What it does
cards.back:
• Device driver | Lets hardware devices communicate with the OS
• Compiler | Translates high-level code into computer language
• Linker | Combines modules into a single program
• Utilities | Manage and maintain computer resources
System software that lets the user communicate with the hardware and perform many basic tasks.

User interface: Lets you interact with the computer
User accounts: Manages who can log in
Peripherals: Manages connected devices
Memory: Allocates RAM to running programs
Security: Protects the system
Files & folders: Create, rename, delete, move

Command Line Interface — the user types commands to interact with the computer.
Advantages:
• Uses less memory than a GUI
• Needs less processing power
• Not limited to pre-set options
• More direct control of settings
Disadvantages:
• Commands must be learned and memorised
• Must be typed in exactly
• More prone to data-entry errors
• Not user-friendly for non-experts

Graphical User Interface — built around graphical items, using the WIMP system.
Advantages:
• No commands to memorise
• User-friendly for non-experts
• No typing, so fewer errors
• Pointer and icons are quicker than typing
Disadvantages:
• Consumes more memory (graphics)
• Needs more processing power
• Limited to the icons and menus provided
• Settings are protected from the user

Dialogue-based (voice) interface — speech recognition; spoken words carry out actions.
Advantages:
• Hands-free (driver keeps hands on wheel)
• Safer than a standard interface
• Useful for people with disabilities
• Voice can identify a person (security)
Disadvantages:
• Complex to set up
• Expensive to develop
• Unreliable — commands often not recognised
• Must be trained; limited commands stored

Gesture-based interface — the body gives commands without keyboard or mouse, using computer vision and image processing.
Advantages:
• Replaces mechanical input devices
• No physical contact needed
• Very natural for a human
• No training needed
Disadvantages:
• Can be activated by accident
• Less accurate than other interfaces
• Only works near the camera or sensor
• Gestures must be learned; may exclude users with physical disabilities

cards.front: Types of computers: what are the parts?
cards.back:
Desktop (PC):
• Non-portable
Mobile computers:
• Laptop
• Tablet
• Smartphone
• Phablet

Communication: calls, messaging, video calls, email
Office: business work
Education: learning on the go
Gaming: mobile games
Entertainment: streaming music and video
Remote control: of other devices

Desktop — large, non-portable computer designed to sit on a desk. Uses: office, education, gaming, entertainment.
Advantages:
• Less chance of being stolen
• Better specification for the price
• Easier to upgrade
• More stable wired internet
Disadvantages:
• Not very portable
• Larger footprint (physical space used)
• Needs constant power — no use in a power cut

Laptop — portable, battery-powered, with built-in keyboard, screen and touchpad.
Advantages:
• Lightweight, portable
• Smaller footprint than desktop
• Low power use and heat
• Built-in battery for power cuts
• No trailing wires
Disadvantages:
• Easier to lose or steal
• Not always possible to upgrade
• More expensive than a similar desktop

Tablet — touchscreen portable device with no physical keyboard (optional external one).
Advantages:
• Very fast to switch on
• Lighter and smaller than laptops
• Simple touchscreen
• Battery, low power, low heat
Disadvantages:
• Less storage than laptops/desktops
• Easier to lose
• Typing on a touchscreen is slower
• Supports fewer file formats

Smartphone — handheld device combining phone, internet, camera, GPS and computing. The most portable computer.
Advantages:
• Most portable of all
• Easy to use on the move
• Can use 3G/4G/5G
• Battery for power cuts
• Usually always with you
Disadvantages:
• Easiest to lose
• Less storage than laptops/desktops
• Small keyboard slows typing

Phablet — a tablet that works as a smartphone; size sits between the two.
Advantages:
• Makes phone calls like a smartphone
• Supports 3G/4G/5G
• Larger screen than a phone
Disadvantages:
• Bigger to carry than a phone
• Less portable than a smartphone

Desktop: None
Laptop: High
Tablet: Very high
Phablet: Very high
Smartphone: Highest

Portability: None
Power: Highest
Main strength: Performance and upgradability

Portability: High
Power: High
Main strength: Portability with power

Portability: Very high
Power: Medium
Main strength: Touch and lightweight

Portability: Highest
Power: Lower
Main strength: Always-on connectivity

Portability: Very high
Power: Medium
Main strength: Large screen + phone calls

cards.front: Which device can be used during a power cut and is easy to upgrade?
cards.back: Trick question — no single one. A desktop is easy to upgrade but needs constant power; mobile devices have batteries but are often hard to upgrade.

title: Chapter 2 – Input Devices
description: How data gets into a computer — from a mouse click to a contactless payment.
subject: IGCSE ICT

cards.back: A device that sends data to a computer for processing, turning input into a form the computer can understand. Under the control of the user.

Analogue:
• Continuous, in waveform
• Must be converted to be processed
• Temperature, sound, light, weight, human voice
Digital:
• Discrete 1s and 0s (binary)
• Processed without conversion
• Barcode, digital watch, light switch

cards.front: Microphone → computer (ADC): what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Sound – Analogue waves
2. ADC – Analogue → digital
3. Computer – Processes digital data

cards.front: Computer → speakers (DAC): what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Computer – Digital data
2. DAC – Digital → analogue
3. Speaker – Makes sound
ADC converts analogue to digital so a computer can read it. DAC converts digital to analogue — to control an external device or send to an actuator.
A device used to move and control the on-screen pointer (cursor).

Used for: Moving the pointer · opening, closing, minimising software · moving and deleting files
Advantages:
• Needs less desk area than a keyboard
• Faster way to choose an option than a keyboard
Disadvantages:
• Hard for people with restricted hand/wrist movement
• Needs a flat surface
• Excessive use can cause RSI

Used for: Moving the pointer · opening, closing, minimising software · moving and deleting files
Advantages:
• Faster than a keyboard for choosing options
• Takes less space than a mouse
• Works with no flat surface
Disadvantages:
• Harder to control than a mouse
• Hard for restricted hand/wrist movement
• Drag and drop is difficult

Used for: Alternative to a mouse for restricted hand/wrist movement · some luxury cars
Advantages:
• Easier for disabled users
• More accurate pointer than a mouse
• More robust (fewer moving parts)
• Needs less desk space
Disadvantages:
• Needs training — not standard
• More expensive than a mouse

Used for: Racing and flying games · simulators · remote control of drones and vehicles
Advantages:
• More realistic than a mouse
• Easier than a keyboard to navigate
• Easier to steer in games
Disadvantages:
• Harder to control a pointer than other devices

Like a joystick, used whenever steering is required.
Used for: Video games · simulators
Advantages:
• Easier than keyboard or joystick for steering
Disadvantages:
• More expensive than a mouse or joystick
• Steering can be too sensitive — unrealistic feel

Used for: Inputting freehand drawings
Advantages:
• More accurate for drawing than other pointing devices
Disadvantages:
• More expensive
• Slower than pen and paper

Used for: TVs, projectors and home appliances from a distance
Advantages:
• Operates devices from a distance
• Useful for people with walking difficulties
Disadvantages:
• Objects in between block it
• Hard with hand-movement disabilities

Used for: Inputting data into applications · typing commands
Advantages:
• Fast entry of new text
• Easy way to input data
• Inputs text, numbers and symbols
Disadvantages:
• Must learn to type for speed
• Slower than direct data entry
• Excessive use can cause RSI
• Large — uses desk space

Used for: ATMs (PIN) · POS terminals if the barcode fails · Chip and PIN devices · numeric data in spreadsheets
Advantages:
• Very easy to carry
• Faster than keyboards for numbers
Disadvantages:
• Small keys can make input difficult
• Not used to enter text
Devices that input data with minimal human interaction. Faster than typing, and errors are reduced (no manual input).

cards.front: DDE devices: what are the parts?
cards.back:
Marks and text:
• OMR
• OCR
Codes:
• Barcode reader
• QR code reader
• RFID reader
Cards:
• Magnetic stripe reader
• Chip and PIN reader
• Contactless / NFC reader

Optical Mark Reader — reads the position of marks on hard-copy forms.
Used for: Multiple-choice exam papers · school registers · surveys · lottery tickets
Advantages:
• Fast for large amounts of data
• More accurate — no manual entry
Disadvantages:
• Cannot recognise printed or handwritten characters
• Marks must be in a specific area
• Faint marks may not be read
• Forms may need manual checks — slow and costly

Optical Character Reader — scans text from a hard-copy document and converts it to digital text.
Used for: Passports and ID cards · digitising documents · number plate recognition (ANPR)
Advantages:
• More accurate than OMR for detailed data
• Faster than typing; fewer errors
Disadvantages:
• Not accurate for handwriting

Barcode — black and white lines of varying thickness representing digits or characters. A barcode reader scans them.
Used for: Supermarket checkouts · automatic stock control · library loans
Advantages:
• Faster than typing product codes
• Lower error rate
Disadvantages:
• More expensive than a keyboard
• Must be close to the barcode
• Scratched barcodes cause read errors

QR code — a matrix of black and white squares that can link to websites, videos or text. Three big corner squares help alignment.
Used for: Advertising · linking to email, website or phone number · electronic boarding passes
Advantages:
• Holds more data than a barcode
• Read from many angles
• Any camera device can scan it
• Faster to scan; can be small
• Can be encrypted
Disadvantages:
• Can be used to transmit malicious code
• More than one QR format exists

RFID reader — reads RFID tags using radio waves, with no contact or line-of-sight. A tag has a microchip (stores data) and an antenna (receives/transmits).
Used for: Stock control · tracking livestock · libraries · passports (biometrics) · car parks · contactless payment · access cards
Advantages:
• No line-of-sight needed
• Very fast read rate
• Read and write
• Scans many items at once
• Reads scratched tags
Disadvantages:
• Tag collision may occur
• Easy to jam (radio waves)
• Signals can be hacked
• Tags more expensive than barcodes

cards.front: How a QR code is read: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Point – Aim the phone camera at the code
2. Decode – The app converts squares into data
3. Result – Data shown or website opens

Magnetic stripe reader — reads the stripe on a card (credit/debit, hotel key).
Advantages:
• No typing — no shoulder surfing
• Faster than manual entry; fewer errors
Disadvantages:
• No PIN needed — less secure if lost
• Does not work at a distance
• Easily copied by a skimmer
• Damaged by strong magnetic fields

Chip and PIN reader — compares the PIN entered with the PIN stored on the chip.
Advantages:
• More secure — PIN must match
• More robust — no magnetic damage
• Chip data is encrypted
Disadvantages:
• Typing a PIN risks shoulder surfing
• Does not work at a distance

Contactless / NFC reader — reads a card or phone held close, using Near Field Communication. No PIN for small amounts.
Advantages:
• Much faster payments
• Shorter queues
• Retailers never see card details
Disadvantages:
• Only small amounts
• Fraud risk — no PIN
• Can be read accidentally or from a distance

cards.front: QR code vs barcode: Data held
cards.back:
Barcode: Less
QR code: More

cards.front: QR code vs barcode: Read angle
cards.back:
Barcode: Must be aligned
QR code: Any angle

Barcode: Slower
QR code: Faster, fewer errors

cards.front: QR code vs barcode: Device needed
cards.back:
Barcode: Special reader
QR code: Any camera + software

cards.front: Which DDE device marks multiple-choice exam papers?
cards.back: An OMR — it reads the position of marks on the form.

Used for: Photography · scanning documents · security cameras
Advantages:
• Cards hold hundreds of photos
• Image seen immediately
• Stored for further editing
• Can recover damaged documents
Disadvantages:
• Images often need compressing
• Resolution not as good as expensive traditional cameras

Used for: Video conferencing · security recording · streaming
Advantages:
• Very high quality video
• Used for online conferencing

Used for: Converting documents and photographs to digital format
Advantages:
• Images stored for further editing
Disadvantages:
• Can be slow
• Quality depends on scanner resolution
Inputs sound or voice into a computer. It uses an ADC to convert analogue sound waves into digital data.

Used for: Speech in presentations · voice-activation systems · speech-to-text software
Advantages:
• Faster to speak than type
• Improves safety in cars
• Used for VoIP and conferencing
Disadvantages:
• Sound files use a lot of memory
• Speech recognition is prone to errors
An input AND output device — input by touching the screen with a finger or stylus. It is not a pointing device.

Used for: ATMs · public information systems · phones, tablets and phablets
Advantages:
• Quick way to select options
• Small footprint
• Improves hand coordination
• No training needed
Disadvantages:
• Limited number of options
• Excessive use can cause RSI
• Screen gets dirty and less responsive

Used for: Selecting objects and drawing on CRT screens (CAD)
Advantages:
• More accurate than touchscreens
• Small — good where space is tight
• Easy to use
Disadvantages:
• Lag when drawing
• Only works with CRT monitors
• Outdated technology

title: Chapter 3 – Output Devices
description: How a computer shows, prints, plays and moves the results of its work.
subject: IGCSE ICT

cards.back: A device that receives data from the computer and displays the results of processed data.

cards.front: Input vs output: Input devices vs Output devices
cards.back:
• Send data to a computer for processing | Receive data from the computer
• Turn input into a form the computer understands | Display the results of processed data
• Under the control of the user | Under the control of the computer
• Design is more complex | Design is less complex

Cathode Ray Tube — the oldest type, large and bulky, uses an electron beam to display images.
Used for: Specialist areas such as CAD · used with light pens
Advantages:
• Wider viewing angle than most LCDs
• Allow light pens
• Least expensive to buy
Disadvantages:
• Heavy
• Large footprint
• More power than LCD
• Run very hot — fire risk
• Flicker — headaches and eyestrain
• Higher electromagnetic fields

Liquid Crystal Display — thin, flat screen using liquid crystals and a backlight. Often called TFT.
Used for: Main output device of modern computers · phones, tablets, laptops, portable games · many offer touch input
Advantages:
• Lighter than CRT
• Smaller footprint
• Less power
• Runs cooler
• No flicker
• Lower electromagnetic fields
• Sharper images
Disadvantages:
• More expensive than CRT
• Narrower viewing angle

Light Emitting Diode — uses LEDs as the backlight instead of the fluorescent tubes in LCD. Newest display technology.
Advantages:
• Thinner than LCD
• Lighter
• Less power
• Runs cooler
• Sharper image

Uses static electricity and toner (powder). A non-impact printer.
Used for: Offices needing low noise · fast, high-quality, high-volume printing
Advantages:
• High quality black and white
• Duplex (both sides)
• Handles very large jobs
• Fastest speed
• Long-lasting toner
• Larger paper trays
• Lower running cost per page
• Quiet
Disadvantages:
• Higher initial cost
• Coloured laser has high running cost
• Toner/ozone health hazards
• Smaller trays than dot matrix

Uses liquid ink (thermal bubble or piezoelectric). A non-impact printer.
Used for: Low output volumes · printing photographs · inkjet technology is also used in 3D printing
Advantages:
• Best quality coloured output
• Lower initial cost
• Lightweight, small footprint
• No toner/ozone hazard
Disadvantages:
• Slower than laser
• Cannot do large jobs
• High running cost — ink runs out fast
• Can smudge
• Smaller paper trays

Uses a matrix of pins and an inked ribbon. The only impact printer here.
Used for: Noisy or dirty places (garage workshops) · quality not important · carbon copies (wage slips) · till receipts
Advantages:
• Best in dusty or dirty places
• Carbon copies / multi-part output
• Good for continuous stationery
• Very cheap to run
Disadvantages:
• Very noisy
• Higher initial cost than inkjet
• Slowest
• Lowest print quality

Produces solid 3D objects.
Used for: Prototypes · customised items (prosthetic limbs that fit exactly, surgical equipment) · parts for items no longer in production
Advantages:
• Easier and faster to make customised items
• Cheaper manufacturing
• Can make parts no longer produced
• Medical uses: organs, prosthetics, tissue engineering
Disadvantages:
• Expensive to buy
• Can infringe copyright
• Can make dangerous items (weapons)
• Potential job losses

Uses pens to produce large, very high quality drawings and diagrams.
Used for: Architectural and engineering drawings · blueprints · cartoon characters · technical design drawings
Advantages:
• Extremely large output
• Very precise line drawings
• Prints on many materials (aluminium, cardboard, plastic, steel, wood)
• Low running costs
Disadvantages:
• Very high initial cost
• Very slow
• Very large footprint

Impact:
• Dot matrix — pins strike an inked ribbon
Non-impact:
• Laser — toner + static electricity
• Inkjet — liquid ink
• 3D printer
• Graph plotter — pens
The cost of operating a device (ink, toner, ribbon, power) — different from the initial price to buy it.

Thermal bubble: Heat vaporises ink into a bubble that pushes ink out
Piezoelectric: A crystal vibrates to push ink out of the nozzle

cards.front: How thermal inkjet works: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Heat – Ink is heated and vaporises into a bubble
2. Push – The bubble is pushed through a nozzle onto the paper
3. Collapse – The bubble collapses, creating a vacuum
4. Refill – The vacuum draws more ink from the cartridge

cards.front: How a 3D printer builds an object: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Model – Make a 3D model in CAD software
2. Slice – Software slices the model into layers
3. Print – Prints layer by layer (powder + binder)
4. Bind – Layers are bound together
5. Clean – Excess powder is removed

cards.back:

cards.front: Which printer can produce carbon copies?
cards.back: The dot matrix printer — it is an impact printer, so the pins strike through multi-part paper.
Projects an image onto a large surface such as a screen or wall.

Used for: Training presentations and meetings · advertising · home cinema
Advantages:
• Many people see a presentation at once
• Avoids needing several networked computers
Disadvantages:
• Expensive
• Difficult to set up (needs calibration)
Convert digital audio data (via a DAC) into analogue sound waves that humans can hear.

cards.front: How speakers work: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Current – Electric current flows through a coil around an iron core
2. Vibrate – Changing current makes the core vibrate
3. Cone – A thin paper cone attached to the core vibrates
4. Sound – The vibration produces sound waves

Used for: Phones and computers · multimedia presentations · reading text aloud for visually impaired users · playing sound files
Advantages:
• Much louder than the original sound
• Good atmosphere in presentations
• Help visually impaired people
• Very simple technology
Disadvantages:
• Can disturb others in an office
• Quality speakers are expensive
• Can have a large footprint
A mechanical output device that produces movement — rotate, close, push or pull an object.

cards.front: Actuator examples: what are the parts?
cards.back:
Electric motor:
• Washing machines
• Robotics
Heater:
• Turns heating on/off
Valve:
• Controls water flow
Fan:
• Controls cooling

cards.front: Why a DAC is needed: what are the steps, in order?
cards.back:
1. Computer – Digital signal
2. DAC – Digital → analogue
3. Actuator – Moves (analogue device)

Used for: Robot arm · spinning a fan · pumping water · washing machines · greenhouses (windows, fans)
Advantages:
• Remote operation (e.g. nuclear reactor pumps) — big safety factor
• Relatively inexpensive
Disadvantages:
• Usually analogue, so computer signals need a DAC

title: Chapter 4 – Storage Devices
description: Where data lives when the power is off — and how to choose the right place for it.
subject: IGCSE ICT

cards.back: Non-volatile storage that stores data permanently. Not directly accessed by the CPU, so slower than main memory.

Definition: Files accessed one by one — must pass every file to reach the target
Speed: Very slow

Definition: Data accessed directly without passing other files
Speed: Much faster

cards.front: Factors when comparing backing storage: list them
cards.back:
• Storage capacity
• Data transfer rate
• Data access time
• Durability
• Portability
• Price per GB

cards.front: Backing storage types: what are the parts?
cards.back:
Magnetic:
• Media: magnetic tape
• Devices: HDD, portable HDD, tape drive
Optical:
• Media: CD, DVD, Blu-ray
• Devices: CD / DVD / Blu-ray drive
Solid-state:
• Media: SD, XD, CFast cards
• Devices: SSD, flash / pen drive, card reader

Storage media: Hardware the data is stored on — e.g. a CD or DVD
Storage device: Hardware that reads or writes the media — e.g. a DVD drive

cards.front: Main memory vs backing storage: Main / internal memory vs Backing storage
cards.back:
• Directly accessible by the CPU | Not directly accessible
• Faster access | Slower access
• Tends to be smaller | Tends to be greater
• RAM and ROM fixed inside | Fixed or removable
• RAM volatile, ROM non-volatile | Non-volatile
• More expensive per unit | Cheaper per unit
• Start-up instructions (ROM), data in use (RAM) | Files and software permanently

Fixed hard disk drive — magnetic storage inside the computer using platters, a read/write arm and heads.
Used for: Storing the OS · system software and working files · real-time systems · file servers
Advantages:
• Large capacity
• Fast data transfer
• Fast access
• Great read/write longevity
Disadvantages:
• Incorrect shutdown can lose data
• Many moving parts affect reliability
• Noisy compared to SSD

Portable hard disk drive — an external magnetic drive.
Used for: Storing backups · transferring large amounts of data between computers
Advantages:
• Large capacity
• Fast transfer and access
• Portable
Disadvantages:
• Incorrect shutdown can lose data
• Many moving parts
• Transfer rate not as fast as fixed HDD

Magnetic tape drive — accesses data serially. Very high capacity, very slow access.
Used for: Backups of large databases · long-term archiving
Advantages:
• Huge capacity
• Very robust — lasts long
• Fast data transfer
• Cheaper per unit than HDD
Disadvantages:
• Very slow access (serial)
• Affected by magnetic fields
All optical media use laser light to read and write data.

Advantage: Cheaper to buy
Advantage: Portable
Disadvantage: Lower storage space
Disadvantage: Slow transfer and access
Disadvantage: Not compatible with all computers
